summary: A proposal for two changes to the IMP-Host protocol defined in BBN Report 1822. The first covers the 30-second timeout when the IMP sends to a Host, declaring an unresponsive Host dead to the network. The second proposes a new timeout for the Host-to-IMP direction. Comments were invited, with installation planned for October 10 absent objections.

eli5.summary: Two new rules for how a network box and the computer attached to it check that each other is alive, so the network doesn't get stuck.

questions: what is an imp in arpanet
subtitle: BBN proposes marking silent Hosts as dead and adding a 15 second timeout in the Host-to-IMP direction.

tldr.problem: Hosts with ready lines up but unable to accept bits, or stuck in a debugging mode, left messages piling up and made others wait 30 seconds to learn the Host was not responding. A busy IMP could also stall a Host's sending with no notice.
tldr.mechanism: The IMP would declare an unresponsive Host dead to the network until it sends another bit, and would notify the Host with a type 9, subtype 4 message if it cannot process a message within 15 seconds.
tldr.outcome: The changes were independent, open to comment, and planned for installation on Tuesday, October 10 unless serious objections arrived.

today: RFC 394 updates RFC 381 and has status Unknown. It is a proposal that invited comments, and it is not listed as replaced.

sections.title: Two Independent Changes
sections.content:
John McQuillan of BBN describes two changes to the IMP-Host protocol, defined in BBN Report 1822 and revised in RFC 381, which this RFC updates. One concerns the IMP-to-Host interface and its 30 second timeout; the other concerns the Host-to-IMP interface and proposes a new timeout.

The two changes are independent in statement and implementation. Comments are invited, and if no adverse comments arrive, they would be installed on Tuesday, October 10. Serious adverse comments would delay action until early November.
sections.eli5: BBN asks for opinions about two separate rule changes. If nobody objects, they happen on a set day.

sections.title: Declaring a Silent Host Dead
sections.content:
Today a Host has 30 seconds to accept each packet of a regular message, and 30 seconds for non-regular messages. If it does not, the IMP discards all messages held for the Host, sends each source Host a type 9, subtype 0 message (Incomplete Transmission - Destination Host Tardy), drops and raises the IMP ready line, sends 3 type 4 messages (NOP), and sends a type 10 message (IMP-Host Interface Reset).

The proposal adds that the IMP also declare the Host dead to the network. On receipt of the next bit from the Host, the IMP declares it alive and begins a 30 second delay while that news propagates. The motivation: some Hosts have ready lines wired on all the time, and others spend minutes in breakpoint mode, so the wait for a reply is annoying and messages are thrown away. A Host should send at least two NOPs when it receives a type 10 message.
sections.eli5: If a computer stops answering, the network box would tell everyone it is away. Then nobody waits around, until the computer speaks up again.

sections.title: A 15 Second Host-to-IMP Timeout
sections.content:
To accept a message, the IMP must acquire internal resources such as a message number and a table entry. If they are unavailable, the IMP waits and the interface is stopped. This is hard on Hosts with half-duplex interfaces: if it takes 30 seconds, the IMP-to-Host timeout fires and the Host loses messages sent to it in the last 30 seconds.

The proposal is that the IMP try for 15 seconds, then send the Host a type 9, subtype 4 message (bits 30, 31, 32 = 100) defined as Incomplete Transmission - Resources Unavailable. No part of the message has entered the network. The IMP takes in the rest of the message, after which a half-duplex Host should start accepting messages and the Host may retransmit if desired.
sections.eli5: If the network box is too busy to take a message, it waits 15 seconds and then says so. The computer can then try again.

references.text: RFC 381, the revision of BBN Report 1822 that this RFC updates.
